extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners of nonlinear time-series analysis and recurrence-plot methods (physics, geophysics, neuroscience, dynamical systems)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, metrics and algorithms for analysing stability and synchronization in nonlinear time series using recurrence plots (RPs), including preprocessing, indices (CPR, JPR, K2), hypothesis testing (twin surrogates), LOS extraction, time-series reconstruction and automated K2 estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum eccentricity as measure of insolation variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximum eccentricity indicates the variable distance to the central star and consequently it is an indirect measure of the differential energy flux (insolation) on the planet. It can be used to determine regions where the variation of this distance does not exceed 50%, corresponding to an eccentricity of e = 0.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use colour-coded maximum-eccentricity initial-condition diagrams to identify unstable orbits (high eccentricity and large semi-major axis produce larger perturbations). Interpret regions with e ≤ 0.2 as having <50% variation in star-planet distance (a proxy for acceptable insolation variability for habitability analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation entropy K2 as predictability/stability measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation entropy K2 is a sensitive measure for the predictability of an orbit and clearly indicates high-order resonances (even when resonances act at relatively low eccentricities, e.g. e ≈ 0.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate K2 using an automated algorithm (see Appendix B.4). Use K2 colour-coded initial-condition diagrams to complement maximum-eccentricity maps when identifying resonances and unstable regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complementary measures (max eccentricity and K2) to quantify orbital stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Both maximum eccentricity and K2 quantify different aspects of orbital stability and complement each other in detecting resonances and unstable regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine both measures when inferring long-term stability and habitability (e.g., to conclude whether planets will last long enough in the habitable zone). Neither metric alone is always sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPR and JPR indices for detecting phase and generalized synchronization
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute CPR and JPR indices to detect phase synchronization (PS) and generalized synchronization (GS), respectively; e.g., transitions to PS and GS were detected simultaneously at a coupling strength µ = 0.6 in the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot indices vs coupling parameter to identify transitions. CPR and JPR are suitable for non-phase-coherent signals where phase estimation is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: MFNN (mutual false nearest neighbors) reliability caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The MFNN method (index P¯−1) is zero for systems not in GS and approximately one for systems in GS, but it may produce implausible results for non-phase-coherent oscillators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on MFNN alone for non-phase-coherent dynamics: in the presented experiment MFNN indicated GS at no coupling (µ = 0) and failed to indicate GS at µ = 0.6 where other indices did. Example parameter settings used: 25,000 data points, Tr = Td = 0.035 s (sampling 2 kHz), dr = 5, dd = 12; P(n,dr,dd) computed at 10,000 locations and averaged. Use with caution and cross-validate with RP-based indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin surrogate hypothesis testing for statistical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: When coupling strength cannot be varied (passive experiments), use a hypothesis test based on twin surrogates to obtain statistical significance of synchronization indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate a large ensemble of twin surrogates (example: 200), compute the synchronization index (e.g., CPR) between each surrogate and the measured partner trajectory, and compare the original index to the surrogate distribution (use rank-order statistics and 99% significance borders). Report p-values (example: original CPR = 0.911 was significantly different from surrogates with p < 0.01). Note that twin surrogates reproduce many characteristics but are different realisations of the same underlying process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing for non-phase-coherent/noisy data (eye-movement example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For noisy, non-phase-coherent signals (e.g., fixational eye movements) eliminate slow drifts by high-pass filtering: ˜x(t) = x(t) − x(t − τ) with τ = 40 ms, yielding trajectories with maximum spectral power in 3–8 Hz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record at adequate sampling rate (example: EyeLink-II at 500 Hz, spatial resolution <0.005°). After filtering, if phase estimation remains cumbersome, apply recurrence-based synchronization measures (e.g., CPR). Document stimulus and recording parameters (stimulus size, sampling rate, resolution) when reporting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOS extraction algorithm and LOS quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step algorithm to extract the line of synchronization (LOS) from cross-recurrence plots: begin at the first recurrence near the origin, then iteratively search in a square window (initial w = 2) for subsequent recurrence points, increasing window size and computing centre-of-mass to place the next LOS point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control parameters: initial window w = 2, iterative window increase ∆w subject to ∆w < dx and ∆w < dy. Quality criteria for a good LOS: the number of targeted recurrence points by the LOS N• should converge to a maximum and the number of gaps N◦ should converge to a minimum. Correlation between LOS-synchronised series correlates best with the ratio N•/N◦. Implementation available in the CRP toolbox for Matlab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-series reconstruction from recurrence plot (algorithmic steps and requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruction algorithm consists of three phases: (I) handle identical columns by removing duplicates, (II) compute set-differences Ni,j and iteratively build a rank-order series by selecting minima positions until all indices are ranked, (III) assign random numbers ranked according to the order to generate a surrogate amplitude series and reinsert removed identical-column values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key requirements: identify indices j1,j2 with Ni,j = 0 corresponding to global max/min as starting point; when minima are non-unique follow specified tie-breaking rule; rank-order mapping of random numbers yields reconstructed amplitudes yi, then xi = y_{rord_i}; finally reintroduce values for identical columns. Follow the nine specified steps to ensure consistent reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin surrogates generation algorithm (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate a twin-surrogate trajectory by (1) identifying all twin pairs in the RP, (2) choosing an arbitrary starting point, and (3) iteratively appending successors: if current point has no twin use its successor, if it has a twin choose between successors of twin(s) with equal probability, until surrogate reaches original length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If triplets occur, proceed analogously by random selection among successors. Ensure final surrogate time series has same length as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated K2 estimation by RPs: normalization and cluster-detection settings
rubrics_metrics.description: To automate K2 estimation from recurrence plots fix the recurrence rate RR (to avoid arbitrary ε choice), compute the cumulative diagonal-length distribution pc(RR,l) for many RR values, and detect the scaling region of ln pc(RR,l) vs l and the plateau of K2(RR) vs RR automatically via a cluster-dissection algorithm performing linear regressions and minimising sum of squared residuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended practical settings: consider only diagonal lines up to lmax (≈10% of time-series length) to avoid finite-size effects; only use pc(RR,l) values satisfying N^2 pc(RR,l) > 500 for reliable statistics; evaluate ~100 equally spaced RR values between 1% and 99% (i.e., ~100 ε thresholds); for cluster dissection choose 2 clusters for ln pc vs l and use the slope of the largest cluster as the scaling slope; choose 3 clusters for K2 vs RR and pick the cluster with minimum absolute slope as the plateau. These settings were found appropriate for automating the detection of scaling regions and plateaus.
